summary: A democratic country in the southern Korean Peninsula, founded in 1948, which industrialized rapidly after the Korean War and influences the world with semiconductors, automobiles and popular culture (the Korean Wave, Hallyu).

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Confucian thought shaped a Korean tradition of valuing ancestors and family without necessarily belonging to a religious body, and together with rapid industrialization after the 1960s, a high level of education and urbanization, it has led many people not to join any religious organization. The 2015 census showed for the first time that the non-religious were more than half, with the highest share among people in their twenties and thirties, partly out of distaste for scandals in large churches and the politicization of religious groups.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1885 Horace Underwood of the American Presbyterian Church and Henry Appenzeller of the Methodist Church arrived in Joseon and evangelized by founding schools and hospitals such as Yonsei and Ewha. During the Japanese colonial period (1910–1945) the churches took part in the March 1st independence movement of 1919, and Christianity was seen as allied with nationalism; after the Korean War it expanded rapidly with American influence and economic takeoff, and the Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul was at one time one of the largest churches in the world.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was introduced to Goguryeo in 372, was the state religion in the Unified Silla and Goryeo periods, and produced famous temples such as Bulguksa. During the 500 years of the Joseon dynasty the policy of "honoring Confucianism and suppressing Buddhism" was pursued and temples were forced to move into the mountains, which is why most of Korea's major temples are in mountain areas today. Buddhist believers today are more numerous among the elderly and in the southeast such as Gyeongsang, and the largest order is the Jogye Order.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: At the end of the 18th century Joseon scholars formed their own faith groups through Chinese-language Catholic books they encountered in Beijing, and in 1784 Yi Seung-hun was baptized in Beijing and returned to preach. Because they refused ancestor rites, Catholics were severely persecuted by the court in 1801, 1839 and 1866, with thousands martyred, and in 1984 Pope John Paul II canonized 103 Korean martyr saints. In the 1970s–80s the Catholic Church took part in the democratization movement, and its improved reputation attracted many believers.

religion.background: The Korean Peninsula originally had shamanism (muism); in the 4th century Buddhism entered Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla via China, and in the Unified Silla and Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) Buddhism was the state religion, leaving cultural heritage such as the Tripitaka Koreana. In 1392 the Joseon dynasty founded the state on Confucianism and suppressed Buddhism, and Confucian rites such as ancestor veneration penetrated the household. At the end of the 18th century Catholicism arrived via Beijing and was repeatedly persecuted in the 19th century; from 1885 American Protestant missionaries evangelized through schools and hospitals. After 1945 South Korea underwent rapid industrialization and Christianity grew greatly, while in recent years, as younger generations secularize, the non-religious have become the majority.

ranking.name: Korean
ranking.description: South Korea is one of the most linguistically homogeneous countries in the world, with almost the entire population having Korean as their mother tongue. After King Sejong the Great promulgated Hunminjeongeum in 1446, Hangul became the script for recording Korean; during the Japanese colonial period Korean was for a time suppressed, and after liberation in 1945 Korean and Hangul became the core of national identity, and October 9 was even designated a national holiday, "Hangul Day".

ranking.name: Chinese (Joseonjok, Chinese immigrants, etc.)
ranking.description: People who use Chinese in Korea include the overseas Chinese formed from the descendants of Qing-dynasty merchants and soldiers of the late 19th century (concentrated in Incheon's Chinatown), and the Chinese Joseonjok (ethnic Koreans from China) workers and Chinese international students who moved in large numbers after the establishment of China–South Korea relations in 1992. Most Joseonjok can speak both Korean and Chinese, and live mainly in places such as Daerim-dong in Seoul.

language.history: The genetic affiliation of Korean remains unsettled, and whether it is related to Japanese is also disputed. In ancient times Korea wrote in Chinese characters and developed methods such as Idu that record Korean with Chinese characters. In 1443 King Sejong the Great of Joseon created "Hunminjeongeum" (the Hangul alphabet), promulgated in 1446, so that even commoners could read and write, but the Joseon literati still used Classical Chinese as the formal script. In the later Japanese colonial period (from the late 1930s) the policy of imperialization banned the use of Korean in schools. After liberation in 1945 Hangul became the official script, and South Korea gradually reduced its use of Chinese characters while North Korea abolished them entirely.

ranking.name: Kimchi
ranking.description: Pickles made by salting napa cabbage or radish and fermenting them with seasonings such as chili powder, garlic, fish sauce and salted shrimp. Its flavor is sour, spicy and savory, and it is almost a required side dish at every Korean meal.
ranking.history: Pickling has a history of over a thousand years on the Korean Peninsula, but the earliest kimchi contained no chili and was mainly salted vegetables. Chili arrived via Japan in the late 16th century (generally thought to be around the time of the Imjin War) and was widely used in kimchi only from the 18th century, and napa cabbage also became common only in the 19th century, forming today's red kimchi. The culture of kimjang (김장), in which every household makes winter kimchi together in early winter, was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2013.

ranking.name: Bibimbap
ranking.description: White rice topped with various seasoned vegetables, sliced meat, a fried egg and gochujang, mixed well before eating; Jeonju bibimbap is the most famous. It is colorful, with attention to the five-color combination of ingredients.
ranking.history: There are several accounts of the origin of bibimbap: one says it comes from mixing the offering dishes into rice and sharing them after ancestral rites, another that it comes from mixing leftovers with rice on New Year's Eve to finish them and welcome the new year, and others hold it was a farmhouse dish convenient to eat in the busy farming season. A late-19th-century cookbook, the Siuijeonseo, already records "goldong-ban". Jeonju in North Jeolla Province is famous for its abundant produce, so Jeonju bibimbap became the most representative version; dolsot bibimbap (stone-pot bibimbap) appeared only in the mid to late 20th century.

ranking.name: Bulgogi
ranking.description: Thin slices of beef marinated in soy sauce, sugar, pear juice, sesame oil and garlic, grilled or pan-fried on a grill plate. It tastes sweet and salty with tender meat, and is often eaten wrapped in lettuce.
ranking.history: Bulgogi means "fire meat", and its predecessors can be traced to maekjeok (seasoned grilled meat) of the Goguryeo period and to the "yukjeok" (neobiani) of the Joseon court and aristocracy. In the past cattle were precious farm animals, and beef could be eaten only by the nobility and at festivals; only after economic takeoff in the 1970s–80s lowered the price of beef did bulgogi become a dish of ordinary families, and it spread abroad with Korean emigrants and the Korean Wave.

ranking.name: Tteokbokki (spicy rice cakes)
ranking.description: Cylindrical rice cakes and fish cakes are cooked in a sweet and spicy gochujang sauce until thick, the most common Korean street snack. It is chewy, and often eaten with fried foods and gimbap.
ranking.history: Stir-fried rice cakes were originally the soy-sauce-seasoned "gungjung tteokbokki" (court rice cakes) of the Joseon court. In 1953, Grandma Ma Bok-rim of Sindang-dong, Seoul, is said to have accidentally dipped rice cakes in gochujang and begun selling red spicy tteokbokki; in the 1970s Sindang-dong formed a tteokbokki street, and this inexpensive snack became hugely popular among students. Today it is Koreans' most representative commoner snack, and has also become popular abroad with Korean dramas and the Korean Wave.

ranking.name: Samgyeopsal (grilled pork belly)
ranking.description: Thick slices of skin-on pork belly are grilled on a grill plate at the table and eaten wrapped in lettuce with garlic, ssamjang and kimchi. With alternating fat and lean, crisp outside and tender inside, it is Korea's most popular grilled meat.
ranking.history: Koreans' eating of large amounts of pork is quite a recent phenomenon. In the 1970s–80s Korea exported the premium cuts of pork to Japan, leaving the cheap pork belly for the domestic market, and together with the rise in eating out after economic takeoff, grilled pork belly became the representative dish of office workers gathering over soju after work. "삼겹살" (samgyeopsal) means "three-layer meat", referring to the alternating layers of fat and lean; Korea has even designated March 3 as "Samgyeopsal Day" to promote consumption.
